Agent reliability · the helper crew

Keeping our agents honest

Six helpers around every AI agent: test it before it ships, sign off each run, block it when it misbehaves, review changes before merge, and watch the apps it looks after.

kagent · agentgateway · kro · GitLab · Grafana · lab-proven, heading to work

This is the short version of the agent-reliability story, told with the helper crew. Each helper is one product. Everything you'll see has been proven in the home lab; the next step is the work install, which the work agent starts phase by phase.
Why we need a crew

Agents fail quietly and expensively

What we saw

  • One run burned 245,000 tokens and wrote nothing.
  • kagent returns many failures as HTTP 200, so monitoring sees a healthy agent.
  • A model hits a 429 and agents keep retrying and paying.
  • One injected instruction and an agent reaches for a tool outside its job.

What we changed

  • Every agent is tested before it ships, and every run is checked before anything acts on it.
  • A misbehaving agent is blocked at the gateway, then released by a person.
  • Every change to agents or routes is tested in a sandbox before merge.
  • Code decides the facts; models explain them; a person decides.
The problem in one slide. Agents burn tokens, hide errors behind HTTP 200, retry into rate limits, and can be talked into using the wrong tool. The crew answers each of those, and the common rule is: code establishes the facts, a model explains them, and a person makes the call.

Sentinel finds the problem, the agent investigates, Warden checks the work, and only then is a ticket written. Assay is the test the agent passed before it was allowed to do this. Guard and Overseer act when it goes wrong. Lookout and config review guard the way in: every change, before merge.

Here is the whole crew. Read it left to right as a day in the life: Sentinel spots something, Assay already tested the agent, Warden checks the investigation, Guard steps in if the agent misbehaves, and the two Lookout helpers look at changes before they merge.
Watch

Sentinel: find it, investigate read-only

  • Code finds the problem in the app (a deterministic check, not a model guess).
  • A read-only investigator agent finds the cause: it can look, never change.
  • Warden checks the investigation; a ticket is written only on PASS.
  • The agents diagnose and report. Fixing stays with a person or a separately approved step.
Proven in the labLive scene on kagent 1.0.0-alpha17 with GLM 4.6: broken app found, cause named (WHISKY_DB_URL), Warden PASS, ticket written. 3 of 4 runs passed; the fourth was correctly rejected by Warden.
Sentinel is the start of the loop. The important design choice: code spots the failure, the agent only investigates, and it is read-only. Nothing is ticketed until Warden has checked the work.
Test

Assay: the test an agent passes before it ships

  • Seeded faults plus a healthy decoy, run through the real gateway.
  • Scored on the right answer, the right tools and the budget, three times in a row (pass^3).
  • A rogue agent that reaches for k8s_delete_resource fails, and the merge is blocked.
  • Runs in GitLab CI; an unprotected branch fails closed.
Proven in the labSmoke and full pass^3 through the gateway on kagent 0.7.13; on kagent 1.x a healthy agent scores 1.0 and the rogue one fails on the delete tool (exit 1 blocks the merge).
Assay is the pipeline test. Same idea as unit tests, but for an agent: real scenarios, a decoy that should not be touched, and three passes in a row before we trust it.
Sign off

Warden: every run checked before anything acts on it

  • A contract per agent: allowed tools, budgets, the report it must write.
  • An independent evaluator agent checks the work; code checks the contract.
  • Catches what monitoring misses: a 200 that is really a failure, a wander of 14 tool calls, a missing report.
  • Only a PASS reaches the ticket; a FAIL routes to a person.
Proven in the labLive on kagent 0.7.13 and 1.0.0-alpha17. The first worker prompt failed 0 of 3 and Warden caught every one; after tightening the prompt, 3 of 3 passed.
Warden is the in-place sign-off. The best evidence it works is the failure: the first prompt failed all three runs, and Warden stopped every one before a ticket was written.
Police

Guard: block a rogue agent at the gateway

  • A deterministic detector: long runs, token burn, forbidden tools, error bursts.
  • Proposes, or for definite offences applies, a gateway deny policy for that caller only.
  • Caps, a kill switch, a never-block list, and a person releases the block.
  • Overseer handles the other failure: a broken model route is switched to an approved fallback.
Proven in the labLive on the lab: the caller went 200 → 403 → 200 after release, and the same caller on another route stayed 200. Overseer switched a 429ing agent to its fallback and the question completed.
Guard is the police. It blocks only the offending caller, only for definite offences, and a person lifts the block. The 200, 403, 200 sequence is the proof it works at the gateway.
Review

Lookout: a first security read of every merge request

  • The CI job sends only project, MR and commit; the agent reads through a GitLab tool server.
  • Leaves one advisory note, updated in place on new pushes.
  • The tool server has no approve, merge or write tools; safety lives in its code.
  • Says PARTIAL when an MR is too big to read completely.
StatusProven against a mock GitLab and once on a real gitlab.com MR. Not yet run from a real CI runner or on the work GitLab.
Lookout is advisory. It never blocks a pipeline and it cannot approve or merge. A human still reviews; Lookout makes sure nothing obvious is missed.
Rehearse

Config review: test it in a sandbox before it reaches every cluster

  • For MRs that change agents, kro definitions or gateway routes and policies.
  • Applies main and the MR side by side in throwaway namespaces, then probes every route.
  • Findings are decided in code; the note must cite every high finding.
  • Our version of AgentShield's idea, moved earlier: before merge, not after deploy.
Proven in the labBuilt and lab-proven on 26 Nov 2026: four MRs, four correct notes before merge, 12 of 12 safety-fence tests, nothing left behind. Independent code review: approved after fixes.
This is the newest helper. Main rolls out to every cluster, so the merge request is the last place a person can stop a bad change. Config review rehearses the change in a sandbox and writes what it found on the MR.
Config review · what the lab showed

Four merge requests, four right answers

MRThe changeNote on the MR, before mergeWhy running it mattered
21New route with its own auth policyLooks safe to mergeProbes: no caller 401, named caller 200, stranger 403
22Policy loosened to any ServiceAccount, agent given a delete toolNeeds changes delete tool (high), loosened auth (medium)The route stayed closed only because a gateway-level policy still blocks strangers: reading the YAML would miss that
23kro definition stops creating the invoke policyNeeds changes policy no longer rendered (high)kro rendered 12 of 13 children in the sandbox
24Same edit, with a reference left danglingNeeds changes kro rejects the definition (high)Merged, the kind would stop reconciling on every cluster

38 to 80 seconds and 12k to 15k tokens per review. kagent 1.0.0-alpha17, kro 0.9.4, GLM 4.6, mock GitLab.

Here is the evidence. Two of these results came from actually running the change, not reading it: MR 22 looked like it opened a route but a gateway-level policy still blocked strangers, and MR 24 looked like a tidy-up but kro rejected the definition outright.
Config review · how it stays safe

The sandbox cannot touch anything real

Fences in code

  • The model passes only the MR pointer; it never supplies YAML.
  • Everything forced into a lookout-mr-* namespace; Secrets, RBAC and cross-namespace references refused.
  • No agent ever runs: kro agents become stand-ins, kagent objects are only dry-run, kro Jobs become no-ops.
  • Anything rewritten is listed in the note as not tested.

Fences in the cluster

  • Two admission policies: the sandbox account and kro's children stay inside lookout-mr-*.
  • Proven live: kro (which has cluster-admin) tried to write into default and to create a real agent; both denied.
  • A janitor cleans up anything a crashed run leaves.
  • At work: a dedicated sandbox cluster with no real credentials in it.
The obvious worry is that applying someone's YAML is risky. There are two layers: code that refuses or rewrites anything that could escape, and admission policies in the cluster that deny it even if the code missed something. Both were tested live.
